span.p: ON THE SERVER - holds the meaning of both
ON THE CUSTOMER'S PHONE - holds two opaque strings, understands neither

div.style: color: rgb(255, 255, 255) !important; display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 200px; text-align: center; width: 200px;

span.p:
the customer id is NEVER transmitted.
Both directions are: client presents an opaque
reference, server dereferences it privately.
That is the whole mechanism. (D4)

div.style: color: rgb(74, 56, 0) !important; display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 200px; text-align: center; width: 200px;

span.p:
why two different strings? The cookie proves who is
using the APP. The token proves this PHONE CALL belongs
to that app session. Cookies do not travel down a
telephone line, so the call needs its own single-purpose,
short-lived credential.

div.style: color: rgb(74, 56, 0) !important; display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 200px; text-align: center; width: 200px;

span.p:
why the token is stored HASHED but the session is not.
Different threat: the token is the one credential that also
rides an external channel (the call), so a database leak
must not yield working tokens. Sessions expire in an hour
and are revoked on logout. P2c made the call side durable and
left sessions in memory on purpose — a signed-out agent costs
one sign-in, where a lost call costs a caller. If sessions ever
become rows they get the same hashing.
